question: How do you structure a RevOps team for a Series B SaaS company?
body:
## Direct Answer

For a Series B SaaS company, structure RevOps as a single centralized team that reports to the top revenue leader — a CRO, VP of Revenue, or a fractional CRO — and owns the systems, data, and process across marketing, sales, and customer success. At this stage you typically need three to five people spanning four functions: systems and tooling, analytics and reporting, deal desk and process, and enablement. That usually beats one overstretched generalist or, worse, three separate ops people buried inside three separate departments. The goal is one source of truth for pipeline and revenue, one owner for the go-to-market tech stack, and one operating rhythm that ties marketing, sales, and success to the same forecast. Centralize now, because untangling fragmented operations after Series C — once you have more people, more tools, and more entrenched habits — is far more expensive and disruptive than building the function correctly while you are still in the thirty-to-eighty-employee range.

Concretely, that means: (1) name a single accountable owner for revenue process; (2) hire a hands-on systems-and-process builder first to stabilize the CRM and lock down stage definitions; (3) add an analyst who can produce a forecast leadership trusts in a board meeting; (4) layer in deal desk and enablement as contract complexity and rep headcount grow; and (5) run a fixed weekly and monthly cadence so the whole revenue org reconciles to the same numbers. If you do only those five things, you will have removed most of the friction that quietly caps growth between Series B and Series C.

## Why Series B is the inflection point

At Series A, most companies run revenue on heroics — a founder-led sales motion, a spreadsheet forecast, and a CRM that only half the team bothers to update. That works until it doesn't. Series B funding almost always arrives with an explicit mandate to scale go-to-market *predictably*, and predictability is exactly what ad hoc operations cannot deliver. Investors are no longer buying the promise of a product; they are buying the promise of a repeatable revenue engine, and they will scrutinize your metrics accordingly.

The symptoms of missing operations show up fast and they are recognizable. Marketing and sales argue about lead quality because they each define a "lead" differently. The forecast swings wildly week to week because pipeline hygiene is inconsistent and reps sandbag or inflate at will. Nobody can state with confidence what a customer is worth over their lifetime, because the data needed to compute it lives in four disconnected systems. Renewals get handled reactively instead of being forecast months out. Every one of these is a coordination failure, not a talent failure — your people are good, but the connective tissue between them is missing.

RevOps exists to build and own that connective tissue. It is the function that makes the handoffs between teams reliable, the definitions shared, and the reporting trustworthy. Series B is the inflection point because it is the first moment when the cost of *not* having that function — in lost deals, blown forecasts, and wasted tooling spend — reliably exceeds the cost of building it. Wait too long and you are not building operations; you are performing surgery on a moving vehicle.

## The four functions RevOps must cover

Think in terms of functions first and headcount second. Headcount will grow and shrink and shuffle; the functions are permanent. A Series B RevOps team needs to cover four distinct areas of responsibility.

**Systems and tooling.** Someone owns the CRM as a system of record — not just clicking around in it, but designing the object model, permissions, automation, and the integrations that connect the CRM to marketing automation, the CPQ or billing layer, the data warehouse, and any product-usage telemetry. This person prevents the slow decay where every rep invents their own fields and the data model turns to mud. They are the single throat to choke when a workflow breaks.

**Analytics and reporting.** Someone owns the numbers: pipeline coverage, conversion rates by stage, sales-cycle length, win rates, forecast accuracy, and the unit economics — CAC, LTV, payback period, net revenue retention — that a board expects to see. This is not "pulling a report"; it is defining metrics rigorously, building dashboards leadership can self-serve, and being the person who can explain *why* the number moved, not just that it did.

**Deal desk and process.** Someone owns how deals actually get done: quoting and pricing approvals, discount thresholds, contract terms, and the stage definitions and exit criteria that govern each funnel. As deals grow larger and more customized after Series B, an unmanaged approval process becomes a bottleneck that either slows every deal or lets reps give away margin unchecked. Deal desk also owns the shared *definitions* — what counts as an MQL, an SQL, a committed opportunity — that keep every team speaking the same language.

**Enablement.** Someone owns ramp and consistency: onboarding new reps, maintaining the playbooks, running training on new products and processes, and closing the gap between your best rep's behavior and your average rep's behavior. At a small team this is informal; the moment inconsistent onboarding starts costing you weeks of ramp time per hire, it needs a real owner.

Early on, one strong operator can and should wear two of these hats — a systems lead who also builds the core reporting, for example, or a process owner who also runs enablement. That is fine and expected. What matters is that you name all four functions explicitly, so that as you hire, each new person plugs a *known* gap rather than duplicating work someone already quietly owns. Naming the functions is what turns a pile of tasks into an org design.

## Where the team should report

RevOps should roll up to the top revenue leader — a CRO, a VP of Revenue, or the fractional CRO steering the function — and not into sales alone. The distinction is not academic. When operations reports only to sales, marketing and customer success gradually stop trusting the data, because they correctly perceive that it is being shaped to serve the sales narrative. The moment that trust erodes, the single source of truth quietly splits back into three, each team rebuilds its own private spreadsheet, and you are back where you started with a more expensive org chart.

A centralized team reporting to a neutral revenue leader keeps every customer-facing function accountable to the same numbers. It also signals organizational priority. If RevOps sits under the CRO as a peer discipline, the company treats revenue process as first-class strategic work rather than back-office administration. That framing is not vanity — it directly affects your ability to win budget and headcount when RevOps is competing for resources against quota-carrying roles that appear, on the surface, to generate revenue more directly.

There is a real debate about whether RevOps should report to the CRO or to the COO/CFO/finance side, and reasonable companies land in both places. The finance line has advantages when the primary pain is forecast rigor and board-grade reporting, and it can lend RevOps more neutrality. The CRO line has advantages when the primary pain is go-to-market execution speed. For most Series B SaaS companies, whose acute pain is scaling the revenue engine rather than satisfying auditors, the CRO line is the more common and usually the better default. What matters most is that the line is *above* any single customer-facing team, never inside one.

## A simple operating model

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Marketing] -->|MQLs, campaign data| R[RevOps: single source of truth]
  B[Sales] -->|pipeline, deal data| R
  C[Customer Success] -->|renewal, health data| R
  R -->|clean forecast| D[CRO / Leadership]
  R -->|playbooks, tooling| A
  R -->|playbooks, tooling| B
  R -->|playbooks, tooling| C
```

The model is deliberately hub-and-spoke. Every customer-facing team feeds raw data into RevOps — marketing sends MQLs and campaign performance, sales sends pipeline and deal detail, customer success sends renewal timing and account health. RevOps reconciles all of it into one forecast and one set of definitions for leadership, and in return every team gets clean tooling and repeatable playbooks. Crucially, no team owns its own private definition of a qualified opportunity, a healthy account, or a committed deal. Those definitions live in the hub, where they can be governed centrally and applied consistently.

The reason this shape matters is that the alternative — point-to-point coordination, where marketing negotiates directly with sales and sales negotiates directly with success — scales quadratically. Three teams have three relationships to manage; five teams have ten. A hub collapses that into a linear number of well-defined interfaces, which is exactly why the pattern shows up everywhere coordination cost becomes the binding constraint.

## Sequencing your first hires

Hire in the order that removes the most risk per dollar, not the order that fills the org chart most symmetrically.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  H1[Hire 1: Systems and Process] --> H2[Hire 2: Analytics and Forecasting]
  H2 --> H3[Hire 3: Deal Desk]
  H3 --> H4[Hire 4: Enablement]
```

**Hire 1 — a systems-and-process generalist.** Your first RevOps hire should be a hands-on builder who can stabilize the CRM, clean up the data model, and lock down stage definitions and exit criteria. That work alone fixes most forecast volatility, because most forecast volatility comes from inconsistent data entry rather than genuine market swings. This person should be comfortable in the weeds of the tooling and comfortable saying "no" to one-off field requests that would re-muddy the model.

**Hire 2 — an analyst.** The second hire leans analytical and builds the reporting and forecasting layer that leadership can defend in a board meeting. Once the underlying data is clean (thanks to Hire 1), an analyst can turn it into pipeline coverage models, conversion diagnostics, and unit-economics dashboards that actually change decisions. Hiring this person *before* the data is clean is a classic mistake — you get beautiful charts built on sand.

**Hire 3 — deal desk.** Add a deal-desk owner as contract complexity grows and as the volume of non-standard deals starts to slow down your close process or leak margin. This role pays for itself the moment approval bottlenecks or unmanaged discounting become material.

**Hire 4 — enablement.** Bring on dedicated enablement once the sales team is large enough that inconsistent onboarding is measurably costing you ramp time. Below a certain headcount, a manager or your best rep can handle enablement informally; above it, the inconsistency compounds.

Resist the urge to hire a senior RevOps *leader* first if you cannot yet keep them busy with genuine strategy. At Series B you often extract far more value from a hands-on builder who fixes the CRM this week than from a director who needs a team beneath them before they are effective. Hire the leader when you have enough function to lead. A common and healthy path is to bring in a strong builder as your first hire, let them grow into the leadership role as the team expands, or slot a fractional CRO above them to provide senior direction until a full-time executive is warranted.

## Building the operating rhythm

Structure is only half the answer; cadence is the other half. A RevOps team with clean systems but no operating rhythm still fails, because the numbers never get looked at together. Establish a fixed cadence early:

- **Weekly pipeline review.** A standing meeting where sales leadership and RevOps walk the pipeline against the same dashboard, inspect deal movement, and update the forecast. RevOps owns the data; sales owns the judgment.
- **Monthly go-to-market review.** A cross-functional session with marketing, sales, and success where the full funnel is examined end to end — lead volume and quality, conversion by stage, win rates, and retention — so the teams can spot where the engine is leaking.
- **Quarterly planning.** Capacity modeling, quota setting, territory design, and tooling decisions, all grounded in the same trusted data set.

The point of a defined cadence is that it forces reconciliation. When everyone reviews the same numbers on a schedule, disagreements about definitions surface and get resolved instead of festering into three private versions of the truth. RevOps convenes and prepares these sessions; it does not simply attend them.

## Common mistakes to avoid

The most common failure is treating RevOps as a sales-support ticket queue rather than a strategic function. If RevOps spends its days resetting passwords and building one-off reports on demand, it will always be reactive and will never get to the systemic work that actually moves the numbers. Protect a meaningful share of the team's time for proactive process building.

The second mistake is over-buying tools before you have process. A bloated tech stack without clear ownership creates more data problems than it solves — every new tool is another integration to maintain and another place for definitions to drift. Buy tools to serve a defined process, never in the hope that a tool will impose one.

The third mistake is decentralizing operations back into each department the moment a team complains about shared priorities. Centralization always creates friction, because a shared function cannot serve every team's every wish simultaneously. But caving to that friction by handing each department its own ops person reintroduces exactly the silos you built RevOps to eliminate. Expect the complaints, and hold the line.

A fourth, subtler mistake is failing to define ownership between RevOps and adjacent functions — finance, IT, and product analytics. Draw those boundaries explicitly so that forecasting, billing, security, and product-usage data have clear owners and clean handoffs, rather than gaps where everyone assumes someone else is responsible.

If you are pre-CRO or scaling faster than you can hire, a fractional CRO can stand up this entire structure, make the first hires, and hand off a running function — a well-worn path for Series B companies that need senior revenue leadership without committing to a full-time executive salary before the role is fully loaded.

## FAQ

### When should a startup hire its first dedicated RevOps person?

Most SaaS companies benefit from a first dedicated RevOps hire somewhere around Series A to Series B, typically once the go-to-market team reaches a scale where forecast reliability and cross-team coordination start to break down — often in the range of a few dozen employees with multiple reps and a marketing engine feeding them. The trigger is less about a specific headcount and more about symptoms: an unreliable forecast, arguments over lead definitions, and a CRM nobody trusts. If you see those, it is time.

### Should RevOps report to the CRO or the COO?

Both are defensible. Reporting to the CRO (or VP of Revenue) is the most common default for Series B SaaS because the acute need is scaling go-to-market execution, and it keeps operations close to the revenue teams. Reporting to the COO or finance can add neutrality and rigor, and is often preferable when the primary pain is board-grade forecasting and financial control. The non-negotiable rule is that RevOps should report *above* any single customer-facing team, never inside sales or marketing alone.

### How big should a Series B RevOps team be?

There is no universal number, but a common shape is roughly three to five people covering the four core functions — systems, analytics, deal desk, and enablement — with early hires wearing multiple hats. The right size depends on go-to-market complexity, number of reps, and how many tools and motions you run. Grow the team by adding a named function, not by adding headcount for its own sake.

### What is the difference between RevOps and Sales Operations?

Sales Operations focuses specifically on supporting the sales team — pipeline, quotas, territories, and sales tooling. RevOps is broader: it unifies operations across marketing, sales, and customer success into one function with a shared source of truth for the entire revenue lifecycle, from first touch through renewal and expansion. At Series B, consolidating these into a single RevOps function is usually preferable to running separate marketing ops, sales ops, and success ops teams that drift apart.

### What tools does a Series B RevOps team actually need?

Prioritize a well-administered CRM as the system of record, a marketing automation platform, a way to manage quoting and approvals as deals grow complex, and a reporting or business-intelligence layer for trustworthy analytics. Add integration and data-hygiene tooling to keep those systems in sync. The specific vendors matter far less than having clear ownership and a defined process for each tool — buy to serve a process you have already defined, not to invent one you have not.

### Can a fractional CRO set up RevOps instead of a full-time hire?

Yes. A fractional CRO is a common option for Series B companies that need senior revenue leadership to design the operating model and make the first RevOps hires, but are not yet ready to commit to a full-time executive. The fractional leader can establish the structure, cadence, and definitions, then hand off a running function to an internal owner as the company scales.
